Accenture (ACN) investors hoping for a 30% jump need Accenture's cash to keep growing even as its revenue growth slows. Increases that large are common for this stock. In 7 of the 10 calendar years from 2016 to 2025, it rose at least 30% at some point. Each rise runs from one close to a later close in the same year, so it can be a rebound from a low. The shares now sit 39.9% below their February 5, 2025 high. At today's price, Accenture's free cash flow yield is 8.1%, against 4.3% for the median S&P 500 company. A yield that high marks either a business on sale or one the market expects to shrink. So what does that much cash mean for you as an owner?

What You Own In Accenture's Cash

As a shareholder, you own a slice of the free cash Accenture produces, whether management pays it out or keeps it. Cash retained by the business still belongs to its owners. Over time, a share price tends to follow that cash, moving faster when the cash is growing.

How Accenture Turns Revenue Into Cash

Accenture earns its money from consulting and managed services. Because its people perform this work for clients, the company needs few plants or machines. In fiscal 2026, managed services brought in $37.3 billion and consulting generated $36.9 billion. Capital spending consumed just 6.0% of the cash its operations brought in, leaving $11.6 billion of free cash flow.

Free cash flow rose to $10.9 billion in fiscal 2025 from $8.61 billion in fiscal 2024. Management said the fiscal 2026 figure was up 7% on that.

Accenture ended fiscal 2026 with $13.4 billion of debt, nearly matched by $12.8 billion of cash and short-term investments. Management said part of that cash came from a $5 billion debt offering in the fourth quarter. Operating income covered interest expense 37.6 times in fiscal 2026. Interest takes little of what the business earns.

What Is Slowing Accenture's Growth?

Accenture is growing more slowly, and much of its growth comes from companies it buys. Revenue grew 6.5% in fiscal 2026, against 7.4% a year earlier. Management said organic growth, from the business it already owned, was about 3% that year. Measured in local currency, management put fiscal 2026 growth at 5%. For fiscal 2027, management guided to 3% to 6% growth in local currency, with 2% to 2.5% from acquisitions.

Management has also named the pressures. In the fourth quarter, it saw lower pricing in many areas of the business. It is also passing more of AI's productivity gains to clients. Management says new kinds of work more than offset that effect. The Middle East business, about $1 billion a year, was a headwind that worsened in that quarter.

title: Stock Market Correction: 1 Investing Move I'm Avoiding Right Now
detail:
Stock Market Correction: 1 Investing Move I'm Avoiding Right Now
Reuben Gregg Brewer, The Motley Fool

IBM
TXN
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The number one thing I don't want to do, at any time and for any reason, is change my long-term investment approach to fit the current market zeitgeist. It is hard to stick to a long-term plan, especially when you believe there's a material risk of a stock market correction. But history shows that while corrections come and go, the market has always resumed its upward march.

This is why, despite my concerns about an artificial intelligence (AI) bubble, I'm not selling either of my two technology stocks: International Business Machines (NYSE: IBM) and Texas Instruments (NASDAQ: TXN). Here's a deeper dive into why sticking to my dividend-centric investment approach trumps the risk of the AI bubble bursting.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
There will be a bear market

I don't know when it will arrive, but I know with 100% certainty that there will be another bear market. And if history is any guide, a bull market will follow, eventually pushing the market to new all-time highs. That's what history shows, and you just have to look at a graph of the S&P 500 index (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) to prove to yourself that buying and holding is a pretty good investment plan.

That said, I am a dividend investor with a value focus. My preference is to buy companies with long histories of dividend growth when they have historically high yields. I believe those two facts indicate a good business and an attractive valuation. That's how I came across IBM and Texas Instruments. At this point, IBM's dividend streak is up to 31 years, while Texas Instruments' is at 23 years.

^SPX data by YCharts

I bought both stocks before the artificial intelligence trade took off, so my decision to jump aboard had nothing to do with that technology. I like IBM because it has an over 100-year history of adapting to the world around it, with a focus on serving business customers. I'm fond of Texas Instruments because it makes boring computer chips that go into just about every electronic device. I would fully expect the two companies to be involved in AI and, in fact, I would be upset if they didn't attempt to benefit from this still-emerging technology in some way.

I'm not getting rid of a good business

To be honest, I'd expect most of the companies I own to find a way to benefit from AI, even if that just meant using it to better serve customers or lower operating costs. But I lived through the dot-com bubble and see similarities to what is going on today with AI, which I believe is in its own bubble. If history rhymes, the bursting of the AI bubble could take the broader market down with it. The truth is, I don't just expect a stock market correction; I expect a prolonged and painful bear market led by the technology sector.

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) booked record networking orders in fiscal Q3 2026, after buying Juniper Networks. That may be what HPE bulls are betting on. Yet the shares fell 17.5% in the month to November 17, 2026. The S&P 500 fell 4.5% over the same dates. Record orders and a falling share price do not seem to fit together. So how much of that networking demand is HPE turning into sales?

HPE Books Networking Orders Faster Than It Ships

Only part of it, so far. On the September 2, 2026 call, management said orders for its networking gear for AI reached $700 million in fiscal Q3 2026. That was up by triple digits. Cumulative orders for this gear reached $2.2 billion, past the company's target for fiscal 2026. So management raised its year-end target to $2.5 billion to $3 billion.

Sales have moved more slowly. Management said networking orders were growing 3.5 times faster than networking revenue. Networking revenue was $2.9 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, up 10% on management's normalized basis. Management said supply constraints limited how much demand it could turn into revenue. Data center networking revenue fell 6%, which management put down to shipment timing driven by those constraints.

Management expects networking revenue to grow 11% to 13% from a year earlier in fiscal Q4 2026, on order strength and better supply. HPE is shipping more networking gear, just not as fast as customers are ordering it.

Can Networking Hold Up HPE's Margins?

So far, it has. Management said gross margin topped 40% in fiscal Q3 2026 on its own adjusted measure. Disciplined pricing in traditional servers and a larger share of networking helped. Networking earned an operating margin of 22%, against 17% for Cloud & AI, the server and AI systems segment. Both figures are on management's adjusted basis.

HPE expects that difference to last. For fiscal 2027, management's framework puts networking's operating margin in the mid- to high 20% range, against about 13% for Cloud & AI. HPE's networking gear is also part of two recent deals. HPE said on its fiscal Q3 call that Oracle will deploy HPE Juniper routers and switches across one of the largest AI cloud build-outs. On September 30, 2026, HPE announced a $1.2 billion order from Vultr for AMD Helios racks with HPE Networking scale-up switching.

The worry for a holder is one management raised itself. It expects gross margin to move back toward more historical levels as AI systems grow and traditional server pricing normalizes, with more networking offsetting that. It also expects the company's operating margin to fall in fiscal Q4 2026 from fiscal Q3. The main causes are a higher mix of AI systems and pricing.

title: IBM or Amdocs: I Can Only Pick One Dividend Stock for the Next 10 Years. Here’s Mine

IBM or Amdocs: I Can Only Pick One Dividend Stock for the Next 10 Years. Here's Mine ©@iJeab via Canva, @nuttapong punna from nuttapong punna's Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Amdocs yields 5.1% after its stock fell sharply on Nov. 4 over a legal dispute with T-Mobile, while IBM yields 2.7%.

Free cash flow covers both dividends well: IBM paid out 43% of it and Amdocs 42% over the twelve months to Sept. 30, 2026.

IBM raised its free cash flow outlook in October, but its dividend grew just 0.6% a year from fiscal 2020 to fiscal 2025, against 10.2% a year at Amdocs.

Amdocs expects free cash flow of $440 million to $500 million in fiscal 2027, down from $562 million in fiscal 2026. That drop is the main risk to its dividend growth.

On Nov. 3, Amdocs (DOX:NASDAQ) proposed a 3% dividend raise in the same report that guided fiscal 2027 revenue down 14.3% to 17.9%. The stock opened down 31% the next morning.

That drop leaves Amdocs yielding 5.1%, close to double the 2.7% that IBM (IBM:NYSE) pays. IBM's news ran the other way: on Oct. 21, it raised its free cash flow outlook for the year.

So if I could only hold one of these dividend stocks for the next 10 years, which would it be?

Source: TIKR and StockAnalysis, at today's prices.

6 safe dividend stocks paying retirees 6%+ yields

There are over 100 stocks paying 6%+ annual dividends today.

But after an extensive investment review leveraging TIKR's proprietary data, we now believe only six of them are truly safe for retirees.

They're all yours as part of our new investment report. Learn more about how to get access right here.

IBM's cash is growing faster than its check

IBM's business is picking up. Third-quarter revenue was $17.1 billion, up 5% from a year earlier, with software up 8% and Red Hat up 11%. Free cash flow came in at $3.0 billion for the quarter, up $0.7 billion, and IBM now expects the full year's to rise by more than $1 billion.

That cash covers the dividend easily. IBM paid out a comfortable 43% of its free cash flow over the twelve months to Sept. 30, 2026, and consensus puts the ratio at 40% for fiscal 2026. Free cash flow has covered the dividend every year since fiscal 2016:

International Business Machines (IBM): free cash flow vs. common dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

The weak spot is the dividend itself. It grew just 0.6% a year from fiscal 2020 to fiscal 2025, from $6.51 to $6.71 a share. At that pace, $10,000 at its 2.7% yield pays $270 a year now, about $285 in year 10 and about $2,775 over the decade. So, call it a 2.9% yield on your cash by year 10.

Debt is heavier here, too: it totaled $63.8 billion at the end of the third quarter, up $2.6 billion so far this year.

Amdocs has a T-Mobile problem

Where IBM's outlook went up, Amdocs' went down hard. Its contract dispute with T-Mobile has become a legal dispute, and the fiscal 2027 outlook allows for either side ending the agreements. Management guides non-GAAP EPS down 26% to 30% for fiscal 2027.
